A performer should never use “inspiration” as an excuse for ignoring the arrangement. A professional performer should know the arrangement, transitions, cues, endings and approximate duration of each piece. Flexibility operates within that framework, not outside it. Imagine a band has rehearsed a song with a specific intro, verse structure, instrumental break and ending. During the performance, the audience becomes highly responsive during the final chorus. The music director may decide to repeat that chorus once before taking the planned ending. That is controlled flexibility. But if the drummer suddenly extends the groove, the keyboardist changes the harmony, the singer adds an unexpected verse and the guitarist begins an unplanned solo, the arrangement can collapse. As a music director and producer, I understand how much coordination exists behind a good performance. Every musical decision affects somebody else. Freedom must therefore be communicated freedom. Prepare rigidly; perform intelligently. Then, when inspiration comes, you can respond without losing control. Preparation creates the boundaries within which creativity can safely happen. The better musicians know their structure, the more confidently they can respond to the moment without losing the audience, the band or the purpose of the performance.
